issues.subcategory: Inconsistent effect size conversions
issues.description: The manuscript reports inconsistent conversions between effect size metrics. For example, it states δ=.11 corresponds to ΔR²=.012, f²=.016, Cohen's d=.25 (from Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020), but earlier in the same paragraph it reports the same study's effect as Cohen's d=.22. Additionally, the conversion from β=.11 to Cohen's d=.25 is presented without justification, and the relationship between these metrics depends on sample size and model specifics that are not provided. The SESOI is described as δ=.11 but this appears to be a standardized regression coefficient (β), not a Cohen's δ, creating confusion about the equivalence testing framework.
issues.quote: we elected to set our SESOI (δ) for our equivalence interval equal to the observed standardized estimate (β value) corresponding to the smallest effect listed above (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent Cohen's d values for same effect
issues.description: The same effect from Grubbs, Lee, et al. (2020) is reported with two different Cohen's d values within the same paragraph. First it is listed as Cohen's d = .22, then later as Cohen's d = .25. These cannot both be correct for the same effect (ΔR² = .012, f² = .016).
issues.quote: small (ΔR2 = .014, f2 = .020, Cohen's d = .24, Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020; ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .22, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)... (β=.11, ΔR2 = .012, f2 = .016, Cohen's d = .25, Grubbs, Lee, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: PGSI scoring error in supplemental materials
issues.description: The Problem Gambling Severity Index (PGSI) response options in the supplemental materials are incorrectly scored. The standard PGSI uses a 0-3 scale (Never=0, Sometimes=1, Most of the time=2, Almost always=3), but the manuscript shows Never=0, Sometimes=2, Most of the time=4, Almost Always=5. This is a non-standard scoring that would inflate scores and is inconsistent with the validated instrument. The text in the methods section correctly states '4-point scale of 0 (never) to 3 (almost always)' but the actual instrument shown contradicts this.
issues.quote: Never (0) | Sometimes (2) | Most of the time (4) | Almost Always (5)

issues.subcategory: BPS scoring error in supplemental materials
issues.description: The Brief Pornography Screen (BPS) response options in the supplemental materials show Never=0, Occasionally=2, Very Often=4, but the methods section states the scale runs from '0 (never) to 2 (very often).' The supplemental materials use 0, 2, 4 scoring rather than the validated 0, 1, 2 scoring described in the text. This internal inconsistency means either the text or the actual instrument is wrong.
issues.quote: on a three-point scale of 0 (never) to 2 (very often). Responses are summed... Never (0) | Occasionally (2) | Very Often (4)

issues.subcategory: Non-parallel measurement across behaviors
issues.description: The study uses validated, multi-item instruments for pornography (BPS, 5 items) and gambling (PGSI, 9 items) but relies on a modified, unvalidated NIDA-ASSIST composite for all substance use outcomes. This creates a fundamental measurement asymmetry: pornography and gambling have dedicated, validated measures of problematic use while substances do not. The authors acknowledge this partially by including NIDA-ASSIST versions for pornography and gambling too, but the primary comparisons across domains are still made with non-equivalent measurement instruments, threatening the validity of cross-domain comparisons that are central to the study's purpose.
issues.quote: Although such an approach is not currently validated for gambling or pornography, given the inclusion of other validated scales to assess these outcomes (see below), including them within the NIDA-ASSIST will not decrement our ability to evaluate our key hypotheses.

issues.subcategory: Moral disapproval measured with single item
issues.description: Moral disapproval for all behaviors is measured with a single item ('I believe that using ________ is morally wrong'). Single-item measures have limited reliability and may not adequately capture the construct of moral disapproval, which could be multidimensional (e.g., disapproval of the behavior itself vs. disapproval of excess vs. disapproval in certain contexts). This is particularly problematic because the interaction term (moral incongruence) is the key predictor, and measurement error in the moderator attenuates interaction effects, potentially biasing results toward finding null interactions for non-pornography behaviors.
issues.quote: For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement "I believe that using ________ is morally wrong" on a scale of 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

issues.subcategory: Heterogeneous moral disapproval across behaviors
issues.description: The construct of 'moral disapproval' likely operates very differently across the target behaviors. Moral disapproval of pornography is often rooted in religious/sexual values, while moral disapproval of illicit drugs may reflect legal/health concerns, and moral disapproval of alcohol may be rare and extreme. These qualitative differences in what 'moral disapproval' means across domains threaten the validity of comparing interaction effects across behaviors. A null interaction for substances might reflect that moral disapproval of substances captures a different psychological construct rather than that moral incongruence is absent.
issues.quote: we will include a series of single-item moral disapproval questions that match previous measures of moral disapproval of pornography. For each substance, we will ask participants to rate their agreement with the following statement "I believe that using ________ is morally wrong"

issues.subcategory: Severely underpowered subgroups
issues.description: The study acknowledges that prescription drug misuse (estimated n=140) and illicit drug use (estimated n=240-480) subgroups will be severely underpowered to detect the SESOI. For prescription drugs, achieved power is only .301, meaning there is a ~70% chance of failing to detect a true effect of the hypothesized size. This is particularly problematic because the study aims to demonstrate null effects (via equivalence testing) for these behaviors, and being underpowered makes it impossible to meaningfully distinguish between 'no effect' and 'insufficient power to detect an effect.'
issues.quote: However, in the case of illicit drug use (prevalence estimated at 6%-12% of the population) and prescription drug misuse (prevalence estimated at 3.5% of the population), it is possible, if not probable, that our final sample sizes will fall below the minimum size required to detect effects that small (See Table 2).

issues.subcategory: Non-representative oversample biasing gambling analyses
issues.description: The gambling sample includes 1,500 sports-wagering individuals in addition to the 2,500 representative sample, creating a combined gambling sample of ~3,325 that is not representative of the general population of gamblers. Sports bettors may differ systematically from other gamblers (e.g., lottery players, casino gamblers) in their moral attitudes toward gambling, frequency patterns, and problem gambling rates. This oversample could bias the gambling analyses in unpredictable ways, yet no plan is described for weighting or analyzing the representative and oversample groups separately.
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically. This will provide us with a total sample of over 4,000 American adults.

issues.subcategory: No correction for multiple comparisons across 10 tests
issues.description: The study plans 10 moderation analyses but does not describe any correction for multiple comparisons across these tests. While Holm corrections are mentioned for bivariate correlations, no such correction is specified for the primary hypothesis tests. With 10 tests at α=.05, the family-wise error rate is substantially inflated, increasing the risk of finding a significant interaction for pornography by chance or failing to find significance for other behaviors.
issues.quote: In total, we will conduct 10 moderation analyses for moral disapproval and frequency, corresponding to the 8 target behaviors/variables of interest, with pornography and gambling repeated for both the NIDA-ASSIST measure and the validate measures of problematic use

issues.subcategory: Conflation of self-reported feelings of addiction with disorder symptoms
issues.description: The study conflates self-reported feelings of addiction (the target of the PPMI model) with validated measures of disorder symptoms (PGSI, NIDA-ASSIST). The PPMI model specifically concerns self-perceived addiction, which is conceptually distinct from meeting diagnostic criteria. Using the PGSI (which assesses behavioral consequences and diagnostic symptoms) as an outcome for gambling but the BPS (which assesses self-perceived compulsivity) for pornography creates a conceptual mismatch. Finding that moral incongruence predicts BPS scores but not PGSI scores could reflect differences in what these instruments measure rather than differences in the role of moral incongruence.
issues.quote: self-reported feelings of addiction to pornography will be assessed using the Brief Pornography Screen... problem gambling behavior will be measured using the Problem Gambling Severity Index

issues.subcategory: Restriction of range due to conditional administration
issues.description: Moral disapproval and problematic use measures are only administered to past-year users of each behavior. This design choice restricts the range of moral disapproval scores, as those with the strongest moral disapproval who successfully abstain are excluded. This is particularly problematic for behaviors with strong moral prohibitions (e.g., illicit drugs, pornography among religious individuals) where the most morally disapproving individuals may be least likely to engage in the behavior at all, truncating the moral disapproval distribution and attenuating interaction effects.
issues.quote: For each target behavior and corresponding measure of problematic use or addiction, key measures will be restricted to those who have engaged in the behavior within the past year. That is, we will only administer measures of problematic use and moral disapproval to participants who report engaging in those behaviors.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent frequency scale anchors
issues.description: The frequency scale is described in the text as ranging from '1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)' for pornography, but the supplemental materials show the scale as 0 (Never) to 5 (More than Once Per Day) for all behaviors including pornography. This 0-5 vs 1-6 discrepancy appears throughout the manuscript and affects how centering and interaction terms would be computed.
issues.quote: participants will report past-year frequency of pornography use on a scale of 1 (never) to 6 (more than once per day)... Never (0) | Once or Twice (1) | Monthly (2) | Weekly (3) | Daily or Almost Daily (4) | More than Once Per Day (5)

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent NIDA-ASSIST item scoring description
issues.description: The methods section states that the two binary NIDA-ASSIST items use a '3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months)' but this is actually a 3-category scale with values 0, 3, and 6—not a 3-point scale in the conventional sense. More importantly, the text says responses to all five items will be standardized and averaged, but standardizing items with fundamentally different scales (0-5 frequency items vs. 0/3/6 categorical items) and then averaging them creates a composite with unclear psychometric properties.
issues.quote: Participants will also respond to two questions... on 3 point scale (0 = No, Never; 3 = Yes, but not in the past 3 months; and 6 = Yes, In the past 3 months). Responses to each of the above five items will be standardized, and an average will be taken

issues.subcategory: Cross-sectional design limits causal claims
issues.description: While the authors acknowledge the cross-sectional limitation, the theoretical framework and hypotheses implicitly assume causal directionality—that moral incongruence causes feelings of addiction. The cross-sectional design cannot distinguish this from reverse causation (feeling addicted leads to moral disapproval) or third-variable explanations (e.g., neuroticism drives both moral rigidity and perceived loss of control). This is acknowledged in limitations but the hypotheses and discussion of implications are framed in causal terms.
issues.quote: moral disapproval moderates links between use and self-reported feelings of addiction, and it is this moderation that represents moral incongruence

issues.subcategory: Flexible equivalence region redefinition
issues.description: The analytic plan includes a contingency where, if results are contrary to hypotheses, the equivalence region will be redefined using the lower bound of the 95% CI from the pornography interaction effect. This introduces researcher degrees of freedom, as the equivalence region becomes data-dependent rather than pre-specified. The exploratory nature of this secondary analysis should be more clearly distinguished from the confirmatory primary analysis, and the implications of this flexibility for interpretation should be discussed.
issues.quote: In the event that, contrary to hypotheses, the effects of moral incongruence for gambling and substances exceed our region of equivalence based on our SESOI, we will conduct exploratory analyses wherein we redefine the region of equivalence using the lower bounds of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate for our pornography outcome.

issues.subcategory: Flexible analytic approach for assumption violations
issues.description: The plan to switch from OLS regression to latent variable models with DWLS estimation when assumptions are violated introduces analytic flexibility. The criteria for what constitutes 'substantially violated' assumptions are not specified, leaving room for post-hoc decisions about which analytic approach to use for which outcomes. Different behaviors may trigger different analytic approaches, making cross-behavior comparisons less straightforward.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate. Similar to prior works... we will construct latent variable models using the lavaan package

issues.subcategory: Missing details on YouGov matching/weighting procedures
issues.description: The manuscript states participants will be 'matched to U.S. representative norms' by YouGov but provides no details on the matching algorithm, weighting procedures, or how representativeness will be verified. YouGov uses a proprietary matching methodology that produces a quasi-representative sample, not a true probability sample. No mention is made of whether survey weights will be applied in analyses, which is critical for claims of representativeness.
issues.quote: Participants will be recruited by YouGov Opinion Polling and matched to U.S. representative norms... certain measures of quality control and responsiveness are guaranteed as a part of their data collection process based on their proprietary data collection standards

issues.subcategory: No plan for handling sports-betting oversample in analyses
issues.description: The manuscript does not specify how the sports-betting oversample (n=1,500) will be handled in analyses. Will these participants be included in all analyses or only gambling analyses? Will weights be applied to account for the oversampling? How will the non-representative nature of this subsample affect the representativeness claims for other behavioral domains (e.g., these individuals may also differ in alcohol use, pornography use, etc.)?
issues.quote: we will also recruit an additional 1,500 adults with recent (past year) history of wagering on sports generally or sporting events specifically

issues.subcategory: Gender operationalization unclear
issues.description: Gender is described as 'binary where 1 = male, and 0 = not-male' for the moderation analyses, but no justification is provided for this binary coding. The YouGov panel data section lists 'Gender' without specifying response options. Collapsing all non-male respondents into a single category obscures potential differences between women and non-binary individuals and may not be appropriate for a nationally representative sample.
issues.quote: gender (binary where 1 = male, and 0 =not-male)

issues.subcategory: Confirmatory bias in hypothesis framing
issues.description: The hypotheses are framed to confirm the authors' preferred theoretical position (that moral incongruence is unique to pornography). The authors state they aim 'to demonstrate that moral incongruence is unique to sexual behavior' and describe the alternative outcome (moral incongruence generalizing to other addictions) as 'especially unlikely.' This framing suggests confirmatory bias rather than genuine equipoise. A more balanced approach would frame hypotheses as competing predictions to be adjudicated by data.
issues.quote: we aim to demonstrate that—consistent with the ICD-11 decision to include moral distress as a diagnostic consideration when applying a diagnosis of CSBD—the role moral incongruence in predicting feelings of dysregulation is unique to sexual behavior, in contrast with other addictions

issues.subcategory: Asymmetric predictions for direct effects vs. interactions
issues.description: The hypotheses predict that moral disapproval will have significant direct effects on self-reported problems for ALL behaviors (pornography, gambling, and substances) but that the interaction (moral incongruence) will only be significant for pornography. No theoretical justification is provided for why moral disapproval would have direct effects on gambling and substance problems but not moderate the frequency-problems relationship for those behaviors. If moral disapproval directly predicts problems, it is theoretically unclear why it would not also amplify the frequency-problems link.
issues.quote: We expect to find that moral disapproval of gambling among gamblers will positively predict self-reported gambling problems... However, we do not expect to find that the interaction of moral disapproval of gambling and gambling frequency will significantly predict self-reported gambling disorder symptoms.

issues.subcategory: Moral disapproval ceiling effects for illicit substances
issues.description: For illicit drugs and prescription drug misuse, moral disapproval is likely to be extremely high among the general population (most people believe illegal drug use is morally wrong), creating ceiling effects and restricted variance in the moral disapproval measure among users. Conversely, for alcohol, moral disapproval is likely to be very low, creating floor effects. These distributional issues could artifactually produce null interactions for substances regardless of the true underlying relationship.
issues.quote: I believe that using illegal/illicit drugs is morally wrong... I believe that drinking alcohol is morally wrong.

issues.subcategory: Temporal mismatch between measures
issues.description: The frequency measures assess past-12-month behavior, the NIDA-ASSIST problematic use items assess past-3-month problems, and the BPS assesses past-6-month experiences. These different time frames create temporal mismatches that could attenuate associations differently across behaviors and introduce systematic measurement error.
issues.quote: participants will report the frequency with which they have engaged in those behaviors over the past 12 months... In the past three months, how often have you had a strong desire or urge... In the last 6 months, have any of these situations happened to you

issues.subcategory: Online panel limitations not fully acknowledged
issues.description: YouGov panels, while matched to population demographics, are opt-in online panels that may systematically differ from the general population in ways relevant to this study (e.g., internet literacy, comfort disclosing sensitive behaviors online, social desirability). The manuscript claims the sample will be 'nationally representative' without qualifying this as a matched quota sample rather than a probability sample, which overstates the representativeness.
issues.quote: This work will make use of an upcoming study (N=4,000) involving a representative sample of the U.S. population (n=2,500)

issues.subcategory: No attention checks or validity indicators planned
issues.description: The manuscript states that YouGov's proprietary quality control is sufficient and that no additional data screening for inattentive responding is planned. However, for a survey covering sensitive topics (pornography, drug use, gambling), additional validity checks (e.g., attention check items, consistency checks, response time monitoring) would strengthen data quality. The authors also state they 'anticipate no unplanned missingness' which seems overly optimistic.
issues.quote: we do not anticipate having to remove responses from the dataset due to inattentive or invalid response styles or due to careless responding. Additionally, we anticipate no unplanned missingness of data.

issues.subcategory: Inconsistent effect size reporting for exploratory equivalence test
issues.description: The manuscript provides two different sets of values for the effect to be used in the exploratory equivalence region. In the analytic plan, it states 'β = .27, 95% CI [.23, .31], ΔR² = .072, f² = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020' but earlier describes this same effect as 'ΔR² = .072, f² = .12, Cohen's d = .69' without the β value. The lower bound of the CI (.23) would be used as the equivalence region, but this is the CI for β, not for the effect size metrics (f² or d), creating potential confusion about what exactly defines the equivalence region.
issues.quote: we will test an alternative model where our equivalence region is defined by the lower bound of the 95% CI for the standardized estimate of moral incongruence in predicting self-reported addiction to pornography (β = .27, 95% CI [.23, .31], ΔR2 = .072, f2 = .12, Cohen's d = .69; Grubbs, Kraus, et al., 2020)

issues.subcategory: Gambling frequency measure too broad
issues.description: The gambling frequency measure asks about 'any gambling behavior' and provides examples ranging from buying lottery tickets to placing bets on esports. These behaviors vary enormously in their addictive potential, frequency patterns, and moral valence. A person who buys a lottery ticket monthly and a person who bets on sports daily would both be classified as gamblers but represent very different populations. The instruction to take 'an average across gambling behaviors' is mentioned but only one gambling frequency item is shown in the supplemental materials.
issues.quote: For the present item, please note that gambling refers to any recreational activity in which money or something of value is wagered, bet, or risked for the potential of winning more money. Examples of these types of activities include: gambling in casinos or online, buying lottery tickets, playing fantasy sports for money

issues.subcategory: Unspecified criteria for 'substantial' assumption violations
issues.description: The plan states that supplemental analyses will be conducted when regression assumptions are 'substantially violated' but provides no quantitative criteria for what constitutes a substantial violation (e.g., specific thresholds for skewness, kurtosis, heteroscedasticity tests, VIF values). This leaves considerable room for post-hoc analytic decisions.
issues.quote: in cases where assumptions are substantially violated, we will conduct supplemental analyses to test the robustness of our models, as appropriate

issues.subcategory: Combining tobacco and non-cigarette nicotine into single category
issues.description: Tobacco products and non-cigarette nicotine products (e.g., vaping) are combined into a single category despite having potentially very different moral valence profiles. Moral disapproval of cigarette smoking may differ substantially from moral disapproval of vaping, yet participants are asked about 'tobacco or nicotine products' as a single category. This aggregation could obscure meaningful differences in moral incongruence effects.
issues.quote: we will include specific mention of non-cigarette nicotine products alongside of tobacco products. That is, we will make it explicitly clear that smoked tobacco products, e-cigarettes/vapes, and smokeless tobacco products are all subsumed by our single question on tobacco/nicotine.
